projects.name: The Collective Service
projects.scope: Website audit, complete rebuild, proposed brand identity and document library
projects.line: Partnership · 2026 · Complete rebuild, proposed identity and a Knowledge bank that answers from 279 documents. In testing before relaunch.
projects.summary: A health-emergency partnership’s library, rebuilt from the ground up so a coordinator on a slow connection reaches current guidance in seconds, with a proposed identity and a Knowledge bank that answers from the library itself. In testing before relaunch.

detailImage.alt: The Knowledge bank page: a box for describing a situation above a picture of the library’s documents grouped by theme.
detailImage.caption: The Knowledge bank on the new site, in testing.

figures.label: Home page as it opens on a phone, against a 500 KB budget. Measured 24 October 2026
Page templates measured against WCAG 2.2 AA. Measured 22 October 2026
Documents read into the Knowledge bank. Measured 4 November 2026

challenge: The Collective Service is a global partnership for risk communication and community engagement in health emergencies. Its website was set up in 2020 as a central library of guidance. It is still the partnership’s front door: the place coordinators and responders go for tools, training and data when they have to reach communities during an outbreak.
Six years on, the site was still shaped by the pandemic it was built for. Most of its library dated from 2020 to 2022, while the emergencies people were working on had moved on.

The people who most need it are also the hardest to reach. In a 2022 survey of people sharing emergency-health course content, poor connectivity was the most-cited difficulty in low-income countries, at 29%, against 8% in high-income countries. The median home page on a phone was 2.56 MB in 2025, which takes about 51 seconds at 400 kilobits per second. That is too long for a coordinator who needs a document now.
The partnership had a recognition problem too. A 2023 evaluation found its name confusing for some and its purpose under-communicated. Its logo was the name alone, so it could not help.
goals: Make every page light enough for a slow connection, with a budget of 500 KB a page.
Bring current guidance to the front and retire what is out of date.
Build a document library with search, emergency kits and redirects from every old address.
Hand the site to the partnership’s own editors, with testing, training and a relaunch.

decisions.title: Rebuild from the ground up
decisions.text: Updating the old site page by page would have kept the structure and weight it needed to lose. So every page was rebuilt: a custom WordPress theme of 30 page templates, a new editing side, and content brought across through a repeatable importer that can be rerun and checked.

decisions.title: Set the weight limit before the design
decisions.text: One rule sat behind the design: when audiences conflict, responders win. So every page had to stay under 500 KB, about 10 seconds at 400 kilobits per second, and that limit was set first, so every template was built to it. Each download also states its format and size before it is pressed, so nobody spends scarce data on a file they did not expect.

decisions.title: Hold every document on the site
decisions.text: Many documents were only linked to, so they would stop working if a publisher moved a page. We fetched 155 of them, so the site now holds its own copies, with French, Portuguese, Spanish and Swahili versions where publishers offer them. Documents listed two, three or four times now appear once, with their other languages on the same page.

decisions.title: Treat the brand as part of the problem
decisions.text: A better website could not, on its own, explain what the Service is. So we made the case for a new identity alongside it. The reasons are set out below, under The brand.

decisions.title: Build for the people who will run it
decisions.text: A library only stays current if its own team can keep it current. The editing side has one form for each kind of content, and each form lists what is still missing before it can be published. Adding a document means pasting its address: its format, size and page count fill in by themselves. A built-in guide shows editors each job, screen by screen.

decisions.title: Try a new way into the library
decisions.text: Search only helps people who know the right words. The Knowledge bank lets a reader describe a situation in their own words and get advice drawn only from the library’s documents, with every point cited. When the library has no answer, it says so.

link.text: It is in testing, and it is the first build of the service we now offer as evidence intelligence →

intro: The new identity began with the partnership’s own evidence, not with the logo. A 2023 independent evaluation, built on 88 interviews, 98 survey responses and four country case studies, found the name “confusing for some” and listed “limited communication about its purpose” as a weakness. It also found that 87% of respondents thought they were likely to need the Service in a future health emergency. So this had to be an identity built to last, and one that helps explain what the Service is.

The existing logo was made to put a name on a pandemic response, and it did that job. It had not been asked to do more. A logo that is only the name cannot explain a name people find confusing, so the identity needed a form that carries the idea: organisations acting as one, so that communities are listened to in an emergency.

reasons.title: It says what the Service is
reasons.text: Three separate parts join one body: distinct organisations, drawn as equals, becoming one service. A reader sees “together” before reading a word, so the mark works on the confusion the evaluation found every time it appears.

reasons.title: It keeps the partners equal
reasons.text: The Service is a partnership of equals. No part of the mark takes precedence, and a single quiet colour lets it sit beside four established logos without crowding them.

reasons.title: It matches how the partners work
reasons.text: Each partner pairs a symbol with its name. The Service was the only member of its own partnership without one.

reasons.title: It works in every language
reasons.text: The Service publishes in English, French, Portuguese and Spanish, and much of its work is in francophone and lusophone Africa. A symbol works in all of them. The name stays in English and the line beneath it is translated.

reasons.title: It works wherever the Service appears
reasons.text: The Service is increasingly found in feeds, browser tabs, group chats and on phones, where a wordmark cannot be read. Solid shapes also survive the stamps, badges and photocopies of field materials. Size was only one test of eight. Both logos were tested on meaning, small sizes, reusable parts, sitting with the partners, matching the voice, reliable reproduction, distinctiveness and whether rules can govern them.

reasons.title: It survives a change of name
reasons.text: The evaluation recommended that the partners consider changing the name. If they do, the mark stays and only the words beside it change.

reasons.title: It rests on evidence, at low risk
reasons.text: A 2019 study in the Journal of Marketing Research, across six experiments and 597 logos, found that more descriptive logos are easier to take in and are judged more authentic, most of all for brands people do not yet know well. The cost of changing is low: the name, where the recognition lives, stays, and the mark is one small file using fonts the site already loads. The risk of not changing is that the evaluation’s findings stay unaddressed at the most visible layer.

guidelines: The identity goes further than the mark. The voice is plain, concrete, calm and honest, because jargon is a barrier to someone in the middle of a crisis. Colour has a job: ink for text, sand for backgrounds, and coral only for what is live now and the one action that matters.

All of this is set out in a 57-page design and brand document, shared with the partnership in October 2026. Part A makes the case and sets the guidelines: the evidence, the side-by-side tests, the cost and risk of changing, voice and tone, construction, clear space and minimum sizes, colour, type, photography, four language versions, use beside the partners and the rules. Part B is the design standard for the website, and every rule in it carries its reason and the kind of support behind it: the terms of reference, published evidence, a computed value, a standard or our own judgement.
The identity is proposed and is shared here with the partnership’s permission; adopting it is the partnership’s decision.

What can be reported is what was tested. On 23 October 2026 a crawl of 332 pages and 634 links to other sites found none broken. Every page is checked from 320 to 1,920 pixels wide. Visitor measurement is built in and loads only after a visitor consents, so the relaunch can be judged on real use.
lessons: Count before you design. Reading the site’s own database, rather than estimating from a crawl, showed how much of the library belonged to another time, and that changed the plan.
Weight is a design decision. Set the limit first and every template is built to it.
Make the case for a brand with evidence. Setting out the findings, the tests and the cost of change lets partners decide on the argument, not on taste.
Show people real pages. Reviewers pinned comments to the working site, so each point was about something they could see and could be tracked to a fix or a decision.

projects.name: Global Girls Foundation
projects.scope: Website redesign, WordPress build and fundraising platform integration
projects.line: Foundation · 2026 · Website redesign and gifts in three currencies. Live since 9 October 2026.
projects.summary: A Swiss foundation created by Plan International needed a site that reads as an institution to a philanthropist’s adviser and takes a card gift in three currencies. Live since 9 October 2026, every page and redirect correct on the day.

detailImage.alt: A section of the Global Girls Foundation home page headed Three ways to invest in girls, with three columns: Annual Giving Fund, Designated Gifts and The Endowment.
detailImage.caption: The giving options on the Foundation’s home page.

figures.label: Currencies for one-time and monthly gifts: Swiss francs, euros and US dollars
Lighthouse accessibility score, live home and giving pages. Measured 4 November 2026
Live home page fully loaded on a 3G profile of 400 kbit/s and 2 s latency. Measured 4 November 2026

challenge: The Global Girls Foundation is a Swiss foundation, established in 2022, created by Plan International to fund its programmes for girls. Its website has to reach philanthropists and the people around them: family offices, advisers and lawyers, as well as family and corporate foundations.
Its website did not match that ambition. It was 11 pages on Plan International’s WordPress platform, hard to manage and to find things on, and it had no integrated way to give.

The new site had two jobs that pull in different directions. It had to read as a serious institution to someone thinking about a legacy or an endowment, and it still had to take a gift by card from anyone who wanted to give today.
goals: Say clearly what the Foundation is and why a donor should give to it.
Give each kind of donor a clear route from first visit to gift.
Take secure one-time and monthly gifts in more than one currency.
Let the Foundation’s own team edit every page without breaking the design.

decisions.title: Offer a conversation as well as a checkout
decisions.text: A major gift usually starts with a conversation. So the first screen offers two routes side by side: give now, or start a conversation. The Annual Giving Fund and the endowment are reached only through a conversation.

decisions.title: Let the donor name the amount
decisions.text: Earlier versions offered preset gift levels. After seeing them, the Foundation asked for them to go, so the giving panel opens with one empty box and sets no upper limit of its own. A gift above what a card can carry shows the bank details instead, and any donor can ask for those at any size.

decisions.title: Keep card details off the site
decisions.text: One-time gifts are taken on the page itself and monthly gifts on Stripe’s hosted page, so card details are handled by Stripe and never by the site. The panel still works as a plain form if scripts are turned off.

decisions.title: Build the editor around the page
decisions.text: The Foundation’s staff needed to run the site themselves. Editors work on the page as it will appear: they change text in place, add sections from a picture menu, and the site checks each page against its rules before it publishes. The WordPress admin was restyled in the Foundation’s own look, with a 31-step guide kept inside it.

decisions.title: Review real pages, not pictures
decisions.text: The design was built as a working review site with comments on the page. The Foundation’s team reviewed real pages on real screens, and only approved pages moved to WordPress.

decisions.title: Move without losing the old addresses
decisions.text: The Foundation’s domain sat with Plan International, so the move depended on its IT team. We sent the exact changes needed, and every old address was set to redirect to its new home. On launch day all 21 pages and 23 redirects answered correctly.

beforeAfter.after: Its own WordPress site, hosted in Belgium

beforeAfter.label: Giving
beforeAfter.after: One-time and monthly gifts in Swiss francs, euros and US dollars

results: The site went live on 9 October 2026, with all 21 pages and 23 redirects answering correctly on the day. One-time and monthly gifts were both confirmed with real payments by 12 October.
For the first time the Foundation can take a gift on its own site, and its staff have been trained to run the pages themselves. Giving totals belong to the Foundation and are not published here.
lessons: Decide who the site is for, then let that settle the arguments. Knowing the reader was a philanthropist made most questions about wording and giving easier to answer.
Expect the giving rules to change. Gift levels, limits and currencies all changed close to launch, so the giving panel had to be easy to change.
When a launch depends on another organisation’s team, send the exact change, not a general request.

insights.title: How to write a website brief agencies can quote accurately
insights.summary: What to count, what to name and what to decide before a website brief goes out, so the proposals that come back can be compared.
inShort: When quotes come back far apart, each agency has usually guessed at something the brief left out.
Count the page types, the content that has to move, the languages and the connections to other systems.
State your budget range and your scoring in the brief itself.
insights.lead: When three proposals for the same website come back far apart, it rarely means that two agencies are wrong. It usually means each one guessed at something the brief left out. This piece is for the programme or communications officer who has to write the terms of reference and then compare what comes back.

body.text: What a terms of reference is for

The United Nations Procurement Manual describes a terms of reference as “a description of the scope of work for services, generally indicating the work to be performed, the level of quality and effort, the timeline, and the deliverables”. It adds that the document is often a vendor’s first and main introduction to what you need, and that clear terms limit the risk on both sides.

The Manual warns in both directions. Over-specification “may increase prices and/or decrease the number of offers”. Under-specification is the opposite failure: essential information is left out. For a website, that second failure is the expensive one. An agency that cannot see how much content has to move will either add a large margin for it or quote low and come back later.
When two quotes differ, ask what each agency assumed. The gap is usually in the brief.
What to count before you send it

items: Page types, not pages. List the templates you need: home, article, document, event, country. Design and build cost follows the number of types, not the number of pages.
What has to move. How many pages and documents are on the current site, and which can stay behind. Count them from the content system if you can, because a crawl misses what is not linked.
Languages. Which ones at launch, which later, whether any read right to left, and who does the translating.
Connections. Name each outside system: payments, mailing list, dashboards, single sign-on. Say who holds each account.
Editors. How many people will update the site, how often, and how much training they need.
Standards. The accessibility level, a page-weight limit, where the site may be hosted, and any data protection rules.

body.text: Say how you will decide

The Manual says solicitation documents must state the evaluation criteria, and that the balance between technical and commercial scoring must be set before a request for proposals goes out. Follow that even if your own rules do not require it. Agencies write better proposals when they know what will be scored.

Then give a budget range. It does not weaken your position. It tells each agency what level of work to propose, so you compare answers to the same question. Hold one round of questions, and share every answer with every bidder.

sources.title: United Nations Procurement Manual (DOS/2020.9), United Nations Department of Operational Support, 2020

insights.title: A performance budget for sites read on slow connections
insights.summary: How to set a page-weight limit before design starts, and how to measure it so the number means something on a phone with a weak signal.
inShort: Set a page-weight limit before design starts, and treat it as a requirement.
We work to 500 KB a page: about ten seconds at 400 kilobits per second.
Measure each page as it opens, scrolled to the end, and on a high-density phone.
insights.lead: Field staff often open a website on a phone, on a weak signal, in the middle of something else. If the page takes a minute, it does not get read. This piece is for teams commissioning or building a site for people in low-bandwidth settings, and it sets out how we choose a limit and hold to it.

body.text: Pick the number first

web.dev defines a performance budget as “a set of limits imposed on metrics that affect site performance”. Its suggested starting point is under 170 KB of critical-path resources and under five seconds to interactive, worked out for baseline devices on a 3G network.

Compare that with the web as it is. The HTTP Archive’s Web Almanac put the median home page in 2025 at 2.86 MB on desktop and 2.56 MB on mobile. On a slow connection of 400 kilobits per second, 2.56 MB takes about 51 seconds to arrive, before any delay from the network itself.

We work to 500 KB a page. That is about ten seconds at the same speed: slow, but usable. It leaves room for one good photograph and a set of web fonts, which matters when the site also has to look like the organisation that runs it.
A budget nobody checks is a wish. It has to be measured, on every release, by someone who can stop the release.
Measure it the way it will fail
A single figure from a desktop browser hides most of the problem. These are the checks that have caught real overruns on our projects:

items: As it opens. Use an empty cache and count the bytes that travel, not the size of the files on the server.
Scrolled to the end. Lazy loading delays images, it does not remove them. A page can pass as it opens and fail by the bottom.
On a high-density phone. Two-times and three-times screens ask for larger images, so the same page can weigh far more than it does on a laptop.
With JavaScript off. Lazy loading that depends on a script stops, and every image on the page may load at once.

body.text: Put it in the contract

Write the limit into the brief, with the method for measuring it. Then each new feature has a price the whole team can see. When something goes over, web.dev gives the three honest choices: optimise it, remove it, or do not add it.
The discipline pays for itself in the first emergency that sends a new audience to the site on phones and poor connections. By then it is too late to start.

insights.title: Accessible colour that keeps a brand recognisable
insights.summary: Why most brand palettes fail only in particular pairings, and how giving each colour a job keeps both the brand and the contrast ratio.
inShort: Brand colours rarely fail everywhere. They fail at small sizes and in particular pairings.
Body text needs 4.5:1. Large text and interface parts need 3:1.
Give each colour a job, and test every pair it will appear in.
insights.lead: Accessibility and branding are often set against each other, as if one has to give way. The real problem is much narrower. This piece is for communications teams and designers who own a palette and have been told it fails.

body.text: What the standard asks for

WCAG 2.2 asks for a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text, and 3:1 for large text, which it defines as at least 18 point, or 14 point bold. User interface components and meaningful graphics need 3:1 against what sits next to them. Colour also cannot be the only way information is shown. Text that is part of a logo or brand name has no contrast requirement.
This is the most common failure there is. WebAIM’s 2026 study of the top million home pages found low-contrast text on 83.9% of them, with an average of 34 instances a page.
Most palettes do not fail. Particular pairings fail.
What that looks like on a real palette

Our own logo uses six colours, one for each language in the display at the top of our home page. Against white, the blue measures 6.16:1, the violet 5.72:1 and the pink 4.84:1, so all three could carry body text. The orange measures 4.30:1, the green 4.38:1 and the amber 3.65:1. Those three fail for small text and pass for large text.

We did not change the colours. We changed their jobs. All six appear at display size and in the logo. All the small text on the site is near-black or dark grey, at 7.23:1 or better, even the small caption directly above the coloured display. The brand keeps its colour, and no one has to read 14-pixel amber.
How to check a palette

items: List every pair: each text colour on each background it will sit on, including hover states and text over photographs.
Mark each pair as good for body text, good for large text only, or failing.
Give each colour a job from that table: text, display, fill or decoration.
Where a colour has to carry small text, darken it slightly rather than replacing it. Readers recognise the hue, not the exact value.
Find what colour alone is saying, such as links, errors and chart lines, and add an underline, an icon or a label.

body.text: Write it down

A palette survives handover when the guidelines say what each colour may do, not only what its value is. Put the table in the brand guide. The next person to build a campaign page will not have to work it out, and the brand will still look like itself.

pages.title: Web design for NGOs and international organisations
pages.description: Research-led web design for organisations publishing in many languages: prototyped early, delivered as a design system that holds across six scripts. A website from CHF 35,000.
pages.statement: Design that starts with who reads the site and ends as a system your own engineers and translators can use.
intro: Most organisations we work with publish in several languages to readers who have nothing in common except the site: a coordinator on a phone in the field, a donor’s adviser in Geneva, a journalist, a ministry. Design that serves all of them cannot start from a look. It starts from a map of who the site is for and what each of them needs to do.

So we research first: stakeholder and audience questionnaires, and a reading of the current site’s own database rather than a crawl. On The Collective Service that count showed most of the library belonged to 2020 to 2022, and it changed the plan before a page was drawn.

Then we prototype the real thing early. You review working pages on real screens, pin comments to them, and approve a prototype you have clicked through before anything is built. Decisions are made on an interface, not on pictures of one.

What you receive is a design system: colour tokens, type, components and their states, documented so that engineering implements it without interpretation and so that it holds across six scripts, including right-to-left. The Collective Service runs 30 page templates from one such system.

pages.title: Web development for slow connections and WCAG conformance
pages.description: Sites built to a performance budget set before design, tested to WCAG by tool and by hand, on an editing layer your team runs. A website from CHF 35,000, fixed fee.
pages.statement: Built for the conditions your readers are in, tested before launch, and run by your own team after it.
intro: A field coordinator opens your site on a phone, on a weak signal, in the middle of something else. The median home page on a phone weighed 2.56 MB in 2025, which takes about 51 seconds at 400 kilobits per second. If a document takes a minute, it does not get read.

So the performance budget comes first. We set a limit, 500 KB a page as a rule, before design starts, and every template is built to it and measured against it on every release. The Collective Service home page opens at 283 KB.

Accessibility is tested the same way: by tool, with axe-core and Lighthouse, and by hand, through the keyboard and the skip link, with the method and the results published in a statement you can file. The Global Girls Foundation’s live home and giving pages score 100 on Lighthouse accessibility.

Then the site is handed to your team. One form for each kind of content, each listing what is missing before a page can be published, with a step-by-step guide kept inside the editing side. Every template, redirect and document migration is handled in the build, so no address you own breaks on launch day.

pages.statement: Your institutional knowledge, queryable, verifiable and compounding.
intro: Every organisation we work with holds more than it can find: years of guidance, evaluations, research, records and the signals that arrive every week. Search only helps the person who already knows the right words. A new coordinator in an outbreak does not.

Evidence intelligence is a knowledge layer built on everything your organisation holds. A reader describes a situation in their own words and receives an answer drawn only from your material, with every statement traced to the passage it came from. When your material has no answer, it says so.

Accuracy is measured, not asserted. Before launch, a set of questions with known answers is scored independently and the result is published with the system. New material is read in continuously, and the benchmark is re-run as the library grows.
It runs on our infrastructure or on yours. If your data must stay in a particular country or on your own servers, that is an option the proposal prices, never a premise.

And it compounds: the same layer extends into working-group spaces, monitoring and briefings, donor reporting and training, so each month’s material makes the next month’s answers better. The first build, the Knowledge bank for The Collective Service, has read 279 documents and is in testing.

pages.description: Identity systems that work at 16 pixels, in a row of partner logos and across six scripts, delivered as guidelines partners apply without us. A website and brand from CHF 60,000.
pages.statement: An identity that still reads at 16 pixels, in a row of partner logos and in a script you do not write.
intro: An NGO’s mark lives in hard places: a browser tab, an app icon, the fifth logo in a row on a partner’s report, a banner printed in a language the designer does not read. Most marks are drawn for a cover page and fail everywhere else. The Collective Service’s old logo stopped working below about 100 pixels wide.

We design identity systems for organisations, programmes and campaigns, and we test them where they will be used. The mark is drawn to hold at 16 pixels and to sit in a row of partner logos without losing itself. The palette gives each colour a job, so that body text meets 4.5:1 and the colours you are known for are kept for display. The typography is chosen across the languages you publish in, including Arabic, Chinese and Cyrillic, so a translated page still looks like you.

What you receive is a set of guidelines that partners and country offices apply without us: rules for colour, clear space, minimum size and type, with the contrast table included, so the next campaign page looks like the organisation without a call to the studio.

pages.statement: A site is only current if someone keeps it current. Four plans, a named person, a report every month.
intro: A library nobody maintains is out of date within a year, and a site nobody updates is a security risk within a month. The sites we build, and the sites we take on after an audit, are kept running by people who know them.

Every update goes to staging before production. On Standard and above, every release is compared against the approved design, so a plugin update cannot quietly change a page. Backups are taken daily and a restore is tested every quarter, because a backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. Uptime, errors and security are monitored, admin accounts are reviewed, and once a month you receive a report that says what was done, what was found and what is next.

A named person replies: the next business day on Essential, the same business day on Standard, within four business hours on Extended and Platform, with an emergency line. Changes within your plan’s hours are made on request; larger work is proposed as a fixed fee first.
Plans are billed monthly, quarterly at 5% less or yearly at 10% less, with a three-month minimum and then rolling. If you leave, you leave with the site, the accounts and the last backup.
